surface_text: An organic additive, Diazine Black (DB), was employed as a leveler for microvia filling using copper electroplating. DB is a derivative of Janus Green B (JGB), which is a common leveler used for copper fill of submicron or micron circuit metallization in electronic products. This study determined the optimal DB concentration for achieving the best filling performance. The electrochemical behavior of DB and its interaction with other additives, such as a suppressor and an accelerator were characterized using galvanostatic measurements. These electrochemical analyses helped explaining the filling mechanism of the plating formula containing the DB. Various surface morphologies and the crystalline orientation of the plated copper films caused by different DB concentrations were characterized by a scanning electron microscope (SEM) and X-ray diffraction (XRD), respectively. The corresponding chemical activity of the surface atoms of the plated copper films caused by different DB concentrations was characterized using a test of etching rate.

surface_text: Because the diameter of the microvia has shrunk to less than 65 -m, and even as low as 50 -m, several metallization technologies such as filling with resin and conductive paste have not met the demands of process integration [1,2]. Instead, researchers believe that a more promising technology is to fill microvia using copper electroplating because this filling technique has been employed successfully to fabricate the interconnections of IC chips, such as via and trench metallization [3–13]. The microvia filling technology using copper electroplating is implemented using a specific plating formula that contains a suppressor, an accelerator, and a leveler [14–17]. The suppressor and the accelerator are basic additives for the microvia filling; the addition of a leveler can significantly improve the filling yield and extend the operative range of the accelerator concentration [16,17].

surface_text: Janus Green B (JGB) is a familiar leveler that bears one quaternary ammonium cation and one chloride ion. It preferentially adsorbs at the protrusion to inhibit the copper deposition rate because of the selective adsorption of the quaternary ammonium cation [18]. Therefore, a proper addition of JGB results in a copper deposit with a mirror-like surface. It is an effective reagent for carrying out a void-free filling in dual damascene metallization [4,5,7,8,10]. With regard to the electrochemical and adsorptive behaviors of JGB on the copper electrodeposition, Li et al. [18] and Bozzini et al. [19] presented detailed results using various instruments to identify the molecular structures of adsorbed JGB and the byproduct thereof. In addition, JGB can interact with polyethylene glycol (PEG) to form a composite suppressor whose adsorptive behavior is strongly convection dependent [16,17]. Hence, the addition of JGB can significantly enhance the filling performance of a plating formula because the forced convection acting on the board surface is always stronger than that at the bottom of the microvia during electroplating [20,21]. The behavior of the convection-dependent adsorption (CDA) of a plating formula has been demonstrated to be an indicator that can determine whether the plating formula is a good candidate or not for the microvia filling [17,22,23].

surface_text: According to the additives’ different electrochemical effects in the electroplating, the additives were categorized as accelerators, suppressors, and levelers, respectively. Bis-(3-sulfopropyl) disulfide (SPS) [3,4] and its reduced monomer sodium 3-mercapto-1-propanesulfonate (MPS) [5,6] are most widely used accelerators. In electroplating, the accelerators can reduce the cathodic polarization and facilitate the copper reduction [7,8]. The suppressors are usually polyether compounds, such as polyethylene glycol (PEG) [9,10], polypropylene glycol (PPG) [11,12], or their copolymers [13,14]. In contrast to the accelerators, the suppressors synergistically work with chloride ions to increase the cathodic polarization and thus suppress the copper reduction. Leveler is another important additive used in the electrolyte to fulfill the super-conformal electroplating, which usually are nitrogencontaining molecules and positively charged in the acid electroplating solution. As reported, the levelers can adsorb at the highdensity charge region of the cathode to inhibit the copper deposition and level the copper surface [15]. In addition, the use of a leveler in the microvia filling electroplating solution can greatly expand the application concentration range of accelerators [16].

surface_text: Currently, most of the reported levelers are nitrogen-containing dyes, such as the Janus Green B (JGB) [17], Alcian Blue (ABPV) [18,19], and Diazine Black (DB)[16] etc., or non-dye heterocyclic aromatic molecules, such as 2-amino-4-methylbenzothiazole (AMBT)[20] and 2-mercaptopyridine (2-MP)[21,22] etc. Because the structure-property relationship of the leveler is not clear yet, the development of novel leveler with high microvia filling performance is very time-consuming and challenging. More and more research groups began to purposefully design and synthesize various nitrogen-containing levelers to study their structureproperty relationship [23–27]. In our previous study, we reported a triphenylmethane-based leveler TPM-1, in which three pyrrolidine rings (nitrogen-containing functional groups) were linked by a triphenylmethane (TPM) backbone [28]. It was found that the small molecule with three saturated tertiary amines already be able to show strong inhibition effect and promising microvia filling performance in the copper electroplating experiments.

surface_text: In this study, a series of novel triphenylmethane-based molecules (TPM-2 to TPM-5) with varied nitrogen-containing functional groups were synthesized and investigated as levelers for copper super-conformal electroplating. The structure-property relationships of the TPM-based levelers have been studied in detail with electrochemical analyses, surface activity measurements, and microvia filling electroplating experiments. It was found that all TPM-based levelers show inhibition effect in the copper electroplating and their antagonistic ability against SPS followed in the order of TPM-2 TPM-4 TPM-1 TPM-3 TPM-5. The inhibition ability of the TPM-based levelers positively correlated to their adsorption ratio on the copper interface. Electrochemical measurements demonstrate that the strongest inhibition effect of TPM-2 and TPM-4 was caused by the synergist interaction of the TPMbased structures and the counter ion I−; the replacement of a fivemembered pyrrolidine ring (TPM-1) by a six-membered piperidine ring (TPM-2) leads to a decrease of the leveler’s inhibition ability; the quaternization of a tertiary amine (TPM-1) with Cl− $\mathrm { C l ^ { - } }$ as the counter ion leads a much weaker antagonistic effect against SPS (TPM-5). Based on the results, it can be concluded that the minor adjustment of the nitrogen-containing group’s structures in a leveler has a significant impact on its electrochemical properties and microvia filling performance. The steric hindrance and the type (tertiary amine or quaternary ammonium with counter anions) of the nitrogen-containing groups need to be comprehensively considered when one designs new levelers for the super-conformal copper electroplating.

surface_text: This work investigated the influence of Sodium 3- (benzothiazole-2 -ylthio)- 1- propanesulfonate (ZPS) as a single additive on performance of copper foil. Electrochemical analysis indicates that ZPS is of accelerating effect during electroplating. Chronoamperometry and ex situ SEM confirm that Copper growth obeys 3D diffusioncontrolled instantaneous nucleation and growth process, with ZPS significantly increasing the density of active sites. A comprehensive theoretical framework combining density functional theory calculations, molecula dynamics simulations, and in situ infrared spectroscopy elucidates an adsorption-capturing acceleration mechanism: ZPS can adsorb on copper surface and “catch” free Cu<sup>2+</sup> to the active sites to accelerate the electrochemical reduction process coupled with adsorbed Cl<sup>−</sup> . Furthermore, a Turing oscillation growth model, supported by finite element simulations and AFM analysis, is proposed to describe the morphological evolution, wherein ZPS preferentially accumulates at valley regions, improving surface flatness through cyclic peak-valley transfer, though with inherently limited ultimate smoothing. Structurally, XRD shows ZPS promotes Cu (220) orientation, while HRTEM confirms the presence of twin boundaries, and lattice fringe measurements reveal a transition from (111)-dominated to (220)-dominated regions upon ZPS addition. Electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) further indicates grain refinement (mean size from 3.29 μm to 2.60 μm) and increased twin-boundary density, which contribute to strengthening via Hall-Petch and dislocation-blocking effects. In terms of performance, ZPS improves surface morphology and reduces roughness. Mechanical properties are optimized at 30 mg/L ZPS, with tensile strength reaching 331 MPa and elongation 3.78 %. Finite-element simulation of high frequency signal transmission demonstrates that the lowered roughness effectively mitigates the skin effect, reducing signal loss. Overall, this work provides a comprehensive mechanistic understanding of ZPS and dem onstrates its potential as a single additive for producing high-performance electrolytic copper foils.

surface_text: In this study, additive Sodium 3-(benzothiazole-2-ylthio)-1-pro panesulfonate (ZPS) has been systematically investigated for copper foil electrodeposition. Cyclic voltammetry and electrochemical impedance spectra indicate that ZPS is of accelerating effect during electroplating. Chronoamperometry and ex situ SEM shows that the 3D diffusion controlled instantaneous nucleation and growth model is not changed but the active sites are increased by ZPS. Theoretical analysis suggests that ZPS can adsorb on copper surface and catch free $\mathrm { C u } ^ { 2 + }$ by -SO<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup> to accelerate the electro-reduction coupled with adsorbed Cl<sup>−</sup> through “bridging effect”. Adsorption-capturing accelerating mechanism was proposed. Molecular dynamics simulation and in situ infrared spectroscopy verify the improved adsorption property of ZPS with increased cathodic polarization. A Turing oscillation growth model, validated by finite-element simulation and AFM, reveals that ZPS accumulates in valleys to locally accelerate growth, improving flatness via cyclic peakvalley transfer, but the smoothing effect is ultimately constrained by this oscillation. Structural characterization demonstrates that ZPS selectively promotes the Cu (220) crystal orientation and suppresses the (200) plane, while HRTEM directly visualizes twin boundaries, with lattice fringes showing a shift from (111) to (220) in twin-vicinity regions upon ZPS addition. EBSD confirms grain refinement (mean grain size reduced from 3.29 μm to 2.60 μm) and a marked increase in twinboundary density, which together enhance mechanical performance through Hall-Petch strengthening and dislocation obstruction. Regarding copper foil performance, surface morphology is noticeably improved, while the optimal mechanical properties are achieved at 30 mg/L ZPS, yielding a tensile strength of 331 MPa and elongation of 3.78 %, attributed to grain refinement and twin-boundary strengthening. Finite-element simulation of skin effect demonstrates that the reduced roughness significantly lowers signal loss. Collectively, this work not only establishes ZPS as an effective single additive for industrial copper foil production but also advances the fundamental understanding of additive-induced structure-property relationships, offering a solid foundation for future additive design and process optimization.

surface_text: At present, the acidic copper sulfate solution is more commonly used for copper electroplating deposition [1], and the main components of the Virgin Make-up Solution (VMS) are copper sulfate (CuSO<sub>4</sub>), sulfuric acid (H SO ), and chloride ions (Cl<sup>−</sup> ) [10]. However, in through-hole electroplating, the orifice of through hole has higher current density and higher mass transfer [11]efficiency than the middle of through hole, resulting in very uneven metal deposition of through hole, which affects electrical signal transmission of the circuit and reduces the service life of electronic devices. Researchers have found that this problem can be solved by adding a variety of additives to the VMS, which has sparked increasing interest in the study of copper electroplating additives [12]. The additives of copper electroplating are generally divided into three categories: inhibitors (i.e. polyethylene glycol (PEG) [13–15], polypropylene glycol (PPG) [16] or their copolymers), accelerators (such as bis(3-sulfopropyl) disulfide (SPS) [17,18], or 3-mercapto-1-propanesulfonate (MPS) [19,20]), and levelers (i.e. Janus Green B (JGB) [11,21–23], Diazine Black [24], Alcian Blue, Safranin T [25], 2-mercaptopyridine [26,27], or 2,2-Dithiodipyridine [28]). With the synergistic effect of the three additives, a bright and uniform thickness of the electroplating inside and outside through hole is obtained. In previous work, our group reported aliphatic amine organics [29–31] and large conjugated molecules [32–39] as copper electroplating levelers, and all of these levelers performed excellently.

Electrochemical tests were employed to explore the ability to inhibit the reduction and deposition of copper ions. In theoretical calculations, molecular orbital calculations of carbazole derivatives demonstrated the ability of carbazole derivatives to adsorb onto copper surfaces. Furthermore, molecular dynamics simulations visualized the adsorption behavior of carbazole derivatives on copper. After through-hole electroplating experiments, the effect of compound Cz-BPDB as a leveler was demonstrated by various instruments. Metallographic microscopy was applied to test throwing power (TP) values. SEM and XRD were respectively employed to observe the flatness of electroplating surface and the dominant crystal orientation of electroplating layer. In addition, to investigate the mechanism of through-hole electroplating, nucleation model theory, molecular properties, and electrochemical properties were further analyzed. This work increased the options for copper electroplating levelers with carbazole materials as a new plating leveler and contributed to the continuing development of the copper electroplating mechanism.

surface_text: In this work, we develop a novel safranine (SA)-based acidic sulfate copper electronic plating process for through-hole copper void-free filling for high-quality electronics interconnection, and both the molecule actions and synergistic effects of safranine (SA) are carefully explored. Cyclic voltammetry experiments at rotating rates of 200 r/min and 1200 r/min demonstrate that SA itself can accelerate the electro-reduction of copper ion, heighten the inhibiting effect of polyethylene glycol (PEG) and acceleration effect of bis-(3-sulfopropyl) disulfide (SPS). The addition of SA to the virgin make-up solution (VMS) containing PEG and SPS makes the relative electric charge (ΔQ) between the low and high rotating rates be increased from 1.27 ± 0.04–22.53% ± 0.05, indicating the higher copper electronic plating amount at the center than that at the mouth of through-hole. In situ Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy together with theoretical calculations further illustrate that the molecule SA is adsorbed on the copper surface through the N atom in the aromatic ring, PEG and SPS can heighten the adsorption of SA on the Cu surface, and both PEG and SPS both synergistically influence with SA to achieve the void-free copper filling of through-hole.

surface_text: The main difficulty in copper filling is the formation of voids in TH with higher aspect ratio due to the uneven local current distribution and tanglesome convection environments caused by the specific geometry of TH [15–17]. The copper deposition amount at the mouth is usually higher than that at the center of TH, resulting in the coating in a void or seam. Therefore, it is particularly crucial introducing the organic additives in the acidic sulfate bath to modulate the copper deposition process at the mouth and center. The key to blind hole filling is the bottom-up growth of copper coating. The key to TH filling is that copper coating rapidly deposits at the center of TH wall until the center is connected to form a butterfly shape structure (two blind holes), and then the two blind holes are filled separately. The accelerator of bis-(3-sulfopropyl) disulfide (SPS) and suppressor of polyethylene glycol (PEG) are the commonly used additives in the acidic sulfate bath [18–25]. Suppressor, mainly distributed at the mouth of TH, inhibits the copper ion electro-reduction at a definite potential which results in the decrease of reduction current density. Accelerator, mainly distributed at the center of $\mathrm { T H } ,$ promotes the copper ion electro-reduction at a definite potential which results in the increase of reduction current density. It is still difficult to realize a void-free copper filling from the bath with only these two additives, and therefore the other additive is further needed. Zheng et al. [12] reported that poly (1-vinyl imidazole co 1, 4-butanediol diglycidyl ether) (VIBDGE) could further heighten the inhibiting ability of PEG in copper electronic plating. Li et al. [13] presented that a copolymer comprising of pyrrole and 1,4-butanediol diglycidyl ether (PBDGE) also could enhance the inhibiting ability of PEG during copper electronic plating. Wang et al. [14] introduced that gentian violet (GVT) behaved with the synergistic inhibiting effect with PEG and the antagonistic effect with SPS. Although considerable studies have been carried out to show the superior performance of additives, up to now, the synergistic action mechanisms of additives are still not clarified.

surface_text: A defect free copper interconnect is crucial for ensuring the electrical connection and transmission of high density interconnect printed circuit boards. Leveling agent is a key regulatory factor for achieving dense cop per super filling from bottom to top in blind holes during the electroplating process of high-density interconnect boards. Here, two small molecule five-membered heterocyclic compounds with different side chains, namely 3- amino-5-mercapto-1,2,4-triazole (AMT) and 2–5-methyl-1,3,4-thiadiazole (MMT), were selected to be as levelling agents to study their effect on the copper filling behavior on blind holes. Electrochemical tests including cyclic voltammetry solvation (CV) and linear sweep voltammetry (LSV) were firstly used to analyze the inhibitory effect of two leveling agents on copper deposition and it was indicated that the MMT has a more significant inhibitory effect on the copper deposition than the AMT. Subsequently, the influence of different concentrations of MMT on the inhibition of copper deposition and the blind hole filling performance were also further analyzed by LSV, CV, and constant current measurement (GM), where an optimal concentration of 7 ppm was obtained for the maximum inhibitory ability on the copper deposition accompanied by the best blind hole filling ability. The characterization analysis from the field emission scanning electron microscopy (FE-SEM), atomic force microscopy (AFM), and X-ray diffraction (XRD) also illuminates that the MMT leveling agent can effectively reduce the surface roughness of copper filled with micropores and promote the selective growth of copper coatings along the (11 1) crystallographic plane. The adsorption behavior of the levelling agent on the cathode surface during electrodeposition was further also studied by the quantum chemical calculations and molecular dynamics sim ulations combined with the in situ electrochemical surface enhanced Raman spectroscopy (EC-SERS) experiments. It has been suggested that the thiol, sulfur, and alkyl groups in the leveling agent MMT molecule are nucleophilic groups, providing preferred active sites for adsorption reactions and thus generating effective inhibition ability on copper deposition formation. Thermal shock experiments based on tin immersion showed the copper layer obtained under the addition of the levelling agent MMT has excellent reliability. The comprehensive results indicated that 2-mercapto-5-methyl-1,3,4-thiadiazole (MMT) was an effective levelling agent for the blind hole supperfilling.

surface_text: Blind hole copper electroplating is the primary technology used in the connectivity manufacturing process for printed circuit boards (PCB), semiconductor integrated circuit (IC) chips, and IC packaging substrates [1–3]. The issue of achieving complete filling of high-quality plated copper has become increasingly essential in light of the progress made in integrated and miniaturized electronic devices. This is particularly relevant as high-density interconnect printed circuit boards (PCBs) are transitioning towards through-hole and micro-hole designs with larger depth-to-diameter ratios [4]. In the process of copper plating on such PCB micro vias with a larger depth-to-diameter ratio, there is a very significant difference between a current’s density distribution inside and on the surface of the micro vias. In such an environment, the copper electrodeposition rate in the pore area will be significantly greater than that in the micropores’ bottom region, which will result in the coppe layer covering and sealing the pore area in a preferential manner, leading to internal defects in the pores. In order to achieve bottom-up superfilling of the micropores, a synergistic effect of different addi tives is required, namely accelerators, inhibitors, levelling agents and chloride ions. Accelerators are generally small molecule organic sul phides containing specific functional groups of (-S–S-), sulfhydryl (-SH) and sulphonic acid $\left( - S O _ { 3 ^ { - } } \right)$ groups, which typically preferentially adsorb at the micropore’s bottom and can hasten the electrodeposition of copper at the hole’s bottom. SPS and MPS are both common accelerator $[ 5 , 6 ]$ . During copper electrodeposition, the inhibitor is usually adsorbed on the cathode surface and interacts with chloride ions to increase the overpotential, thereby achieving the inhibitory effect on the surface deposition of copper, Inhibitors are mainly macromolecular polyether or polyols [7]. The most prevalent inhibitors are polyethylene glycol (PEG), but in addition to PEG there are also polypropylene glycol (PPG) and triblock copolymers of PEG and PPG [8–10]. Levelling agents can be added in very small amounts compared to inhibitors to achieve a strong inhibiting effect and rapid deactivation, leaving the surface flat and smooth. Meantime, levelling agents also show an inhibiting effect o copper deposition but there is no substitute for inhibitors, which can be compared to short-acting inhibitors, while inhibitors show a moderate inhibiting effect and deactivate slowly, and throughout the plating process, the levelling agent gradually covers the copper surface, domi nating the completion of superconformal deposition [4,7]. surface_text: In summary, two small five-membered heterocyclic compounds with different side chains, namely AMT and MMT, were selected as electroplated copper levelling agents in this paper. Therefore, plating solutions often contain various additives for auxiliary plating, including Cl<sup>−</sup>, accelerators, inhibitors, and leveling agents to improve the plating performance of copper sulfate plating solutions and meet the plating requirements of diferent scales and diferent conditions to obtain an ideal copper plating layer.<sup>4−7</sup> Research at home and abroad mainly focuses on organic additives, such as accelerators and inhibitors. Additionally, dye leveling agents such as Jenner green B (JGB) have been studied extensively and organic amine leveling agents are novel leveling agents that have started attracting significant attention.<sup>8−11</sup> Dow et al. considered that the convection-dependent adsorption behavior of a plating solution can be used as an indicator to determine whether the plating solution is suitable for micropore filling<sup>12</sup> and Chang et al.<sup>13</sup> studied the leveling efect of 2-mercaptopyridine. It was determined that 2-mercaptopyridine has a stronger inhibitory efect on Cu deposition than JGB. Considering the complexity and broad variety of chip processes, there are diferences between the plating solutions used for diferent plating processes, plating machines, and semiconductor manufacturers. As a result, plating solutions are typically customized develop ment products. However, there are three main issues associated with the research on leveling agents both domestically and internationally. First, current research mostly uses theoretical calculations, electrochemical methods, and electroplating experiments to investigate the mechanisms and efects of electroplating additives. Unlike traditional electrodeposition, chip copper interconnection involves precise deposition in a narrow space or surface at the micronano level. The morphology and uniformity of the copper deposition layer have a direct impact on the electrical performance of the copper interconnection line, thereby influencing the overall chip performance.<sup>14,15</sup> Its characteristics mainly include small electroplating dimensions, dificulty in filling microholes with uneven current density, and high coating quality requirements. However, there is a distinct lack of comprehensive research on electroplating with structured wafers, which renders most research results unable to be applied in practice. Second, copper sulfate electroplating leveling agents are primarily composed of dye organic polymers such as JGB, which tend to generate significant pollution. With the development of wafer-level, system-level, and 3D packaging, the performance ofelectroplating additives is facing increased scrutiny and evaluation. As a result, the industry is urgently requiring the development of novel electroplating leveling agents. Third, the majority of the existing research is focused on developing independent research models for wafer surface wiring and through-hole filling. However, in practical IC manufacturing, through-hole filling and wiring are performed concurrently, which causes a gap between study findings and application.<sup>16−18</sup> Therefore, it is crucial to develop an application-based screening and evaluation strategy for electroplating additives.

In the first stage, cobalt atoms are electrodeposited on the bottom of the hole and then grow along the wall of the hole with the formation of the cobalt nanoparticles layer. surface_text: ABSTRACT: Electrodeposition technology is the key core technology for achieving micro/nanoscale interconnection in high-end chip manufacturing. Recently, cobalt interconnect structures have been the ideal choice for constructing electronic pathways in process nodes below 14 nm due to the fact that cobalt has a smaller electron mean free path compared to copper; thus, studying the electroplating filling behavior of cobalt in micronano scale space has become a hot topic in the field of chip manufacturing. In this article, an electroplating solution containing a new 5-alkynylpyrimidine (5-EP) as an inhibitor is designed for electrochemical tests, including cyclic voltammetry and linear sweep voltammetry. The results indicate that the 5-EP significantly inhibits cobalt electrodeposition. The change in the nucleation mode of cobalt in an electroplating solution with the inhibitor (5-EP) was revealed by chronoamperometry, where cobalt atoms nucleate in a three-dimensional continuous manner instead of three-dimensional instantaneous nucleation. In situ enhanced Raman spectroscopy is used to further analyze the adsorption of the inhibitor (5-EP) molecules on the cobalt surface during the electroplating process from a spectroscopic perspective. The energy gap value of the additive molecule obtained through quantum chemical calculations is $\begin{array} { r } { \triangle E = E _ { \mathrm { L U M O } } - \bar { E _ { \mathrm { H O M O } } } = 3 . 3 0 2 ~ \mathrm { e V } , } \end{array}$ indicating that the additive molecule has high reactivity and higher adsorption strength at the metal interface. The calculated electrostatic potential (ESP) values of the molecule range from a minimum of −47.29 kJ/mol to a maximum of 70.89 kJ/mol. Lower ESP values imply higher electron density. Molecular dynamics simulations calculate the adsorption energy of the additive molecule (5-EP) on Co(100) to be −133.96 kcal/mol, indicating that the 5-EP molecule has good adsorption capability. Electroplating experiments reveal that the addition of 6 ppm 5-EP to the plating solution enables defect-free filling of blind holes. Finally, it is also revealed by characterization tests (scanning electron microscopy/atomic force microscopy/X-ray difraction) that the inhibitor (5-EP) efectively reduces the surface roughness of the cobalt coating and, meantime, promotes the preferential growth of cobalt along the 100 and 110 crystal planes.

surface_text: Damascene copper plating technology has remained the best choice for metal interconnects in logic chips and memory chips.<sup>1</sup> As semiconductor processes advance toward 10 nm and below, the use of copper as a conductor material begins to encounter issues with RC delay, which severely impacts the interconnect performance of chips. This has led to bottlenecks in process technology at the 10- and 7-nanometer nodes,<sup>2,3</sup> necessitating the search for new alternative interconnect materials. Researchers have found that metals such as Co, Ni, Mo, and Nb show greater potential than Cu.<sup>4</sup> However, when considering other parameters such as process and material costs, only Co is highlighted as a promising material. It has been reported that Co has already been used in the contact interconnect layers at the 10 nm node and is also considered suitable for use as a conductor in higher metal layers.<sup>5</sup> Compared to copper, cobalt has a shorter mean free path for electrons and a higher melting point. At the nanoscale, cobalt interconnects exhibit minimal size efects and superior resistance to electromigration.<sup>6</sup> The deposition quality of chip interconnect materials has a crucial impact on the final performance of the chip, directly afecting the chip’s yield, reliability, and stability. This places higher demands on the chip interconnect process. Electroplating technology is the primary technique for forming micro and nano interconnect structures.<sup>7</sup> In this complex process, additives play a critical role in regulating the deposition quality and behavior of metals.<sup>8</sup> Similar to the traditional Damascene copper interconnect process, the cobalt interconnect plating system also requires additives that can increase the metal deposition overpotential to achieve void-free superfilling in micro and nano structures.<sup>9</sup> The cobalt superfilling additives reported to date often contain unsaturated carbon bonds, nitrogencontaining functional groups, or a combination of both. The nitrogen-containing functional groups exist in the forms of amines $( - \mathrm { N H } _ { 2 } , \mathsf { \Gamma } - \mathrm { N H } )$ , oxime groups $( - \mathrm { C = N - O H } )$ and nitrogen-containing heterocycles. Utilizing the S-shaped negative diferential resistance (S-NDR) mechanism for ultraconformal deposition, Mofat et al.<sup>10</sup> observed bottom up filling of cobalt in 8 μm × 56 μm silicon through-holes. They achieved this by utilizing polyethylenimine (PEI) as an inhibitor. surface_text: To meet the high-performance demands of current electronic devices, copper electroplating in blind vias must achieve flawless filling without cracks and gaps. This typically involves superfilling or botom-up filling techniques, where superfilling refers to a deposition process during electroplating in which the copper deposition rate at the botom of the blind vias is significantly higher than at the opening and surface, thereby achieving perfect filling of the vias [5]. To accomplish superfilling, an acidic copper sulfate system is com monly used in industrial applications. In this system, the choice of additives is crucial, primarily including accelerators, suppressors, and leveling agents. Accelerators, usually sulfur-containing organic compounds, adsorb on the electrode surface, refine the copper crystal structure, and promote copper nucleation. Their primary function is to combine with chloride ions to achieve depolarization, thus increasing the cathodic current density [6–9]. The most widely studied and used accelerators include SPS and MPS [10, 11]. Sup pressors, such as polyether polymers (e.g., PEG and PPG) [12–14], mainly inhibit the deposition of copper during electroplating by adsorbing on the surface of the plated parts and preventing the difusion of ${ \mathrm { C u } } ^ { 2 + }$ [15–17]. In systems containing both accelerators and suppressors, the role of leveling agents is indispensable. Leveling agents typically include certain nitrogencontaining organic compounds [18, 19], such as the dye-type leveling agents JGB [20], DB [18], ABPV [21, 22], and heterocyclic non-dye leveling agents such as 2-amino-4-methylbenzothiazole [23] (AMBT) and 2-mercaptopyridine [24, 25] (2-MP). Their main func tion is to work synergistically with suppressors to inhibit copper deposition on the surface of the plated parts, optimize current density distribution, enhance filling eficiency, and thereby prevent premature hole sealing that leads to voids [25–30]. Although the most efective leveling agents are often commercial secrets, high costs and poor environmental friendliness in the market make the development of new leveling agents both time-consuming and labor-intensive. Consequently, to date, only a few superfilling leveling agents have been specifically reported [31–33].

surface_text: In summary, we have selected the nitrogen-heterocyclic compound CDT as an electroplating leveling agent for copper micro-via filling. The synthesis of CDT was successfully confirmed by infrared, hydrogen nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy, and gel permeation chromatography results. Quantum chemical simulations suggest that CDT possesses the potential to occupy metal vacant orbitals for adsorption. Moreover, molecular dynamics simulations indicate that CDT exhibits strong affinity for copper surfaces. Electrochemical tests revealed that the optimal working concentration of CDT is 5 mg/L. Chronopotentiometric measurements further demonstrated that CDT can synergistically suppress copper deposition when combined with other additives, exhibiting a potential diference as high as 20 mV, which indicates its strong inhibitory efect on copper electrodeposition. Electroplating tests show that the best plating results occur at a concentration of 5 mg/L, consistent with electrochemical findings. Field-emission scanning electron microscopy (FE-SEM) results showed that CDT can refine copper grain structures within an appropriate concentration range; however, when the concentration exceeds the optimal level, crystal agglomeration reoccurs. X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) confirmed the efective adsorption of CDT on the copper surface, and the strong interaction between them provides a foundation for the suppression of copper deposition. Collectively, our research conclusively proves that CDT is a promising leveling agent for copper micro-via filling, providing theoretical guidance for the discovery and improvement of electroplating technologies for micro-via filling.

In the current research on electroplating additives, electroplating levelers have attracted much attention due to their irreplaceable properties. The leveler is mainly adsorbed on the surface of TH and inhibits the deposition of copper ions on the surface of TH, but has less inhibition on the deposition of copper ions inside TH, so as to achieve the effect of conductive copper interconnection or bottom-up copper electroplating [17–19]. The current research on levelers mainly includes the research of new leveler molecules (small molecule compounds [20–22], quaternary ammonium compounds [23–26] and macromolecular polymers [27,28]), interaction of different electroplating additives [29] and the effect of leveler concentration on filling efficiency and copper electroplating surface morphology [30]. Among them, quaternary ammonium salts have received more attention as leveler due to their superior leveling performance. For example, Myung JunKim [31] synthesized choline-based quaternary ammonium salt levelers and used them in TSV (Through Silicon Via) electrodeposition copper, Jinge Lv [32] designed and synthesized three water-soluble naphthalimide derivatives (NPI) and used them as levelers for microporous electrodeposition. Van Quy Dinh [33] used sulfonated diallyl dimethyl ammonium bromide copol ymer to fill the TSV bottom-up electrodeposition for 5 min to achieve no gaps. These studies have shown that quaternary ammonium compounds have good application prospects in the field of electroplating levelers, but it is still a difficult task to develop electroplating levelers with small additive amount, good leveling effect and environmental friendliness.

surface_text: Abstract: Levelers are indispensable additives for achieving void-free, bottom-up superconformal copper filling of microvias. Establishing the molecular-level correlation between leveler structure and performance is therefore essential to the continued advancement of microelectronic copper-plating technology. Herein, nitro blue tetrazolium chloride (NBT) is identified as an efficient leveler for copper microvia superfilling. A multiscale strategy—combining electrochemical measurements, X-ray photoelectron spec troscopy (XPS), density functional theory (DFT) calculations, and molecular dynamics (MD) simulations—is employed to elucidate the action mechanism of NBT and pinpoint its electroactive sites. Electrochemical tests show that NBT markedly suppresses copper deposition and, together with polyethylene glycol (PEG), effectively resists competitive ad sorption by bis-(3-sulfopropyl) disulfide (SPS), thereby enhancing the microvia superfilling performance of the PEG–SPS–NBT additive system. DFT results reveal that the nitro groups and tetrazolium rings constitute the primary adsorption centers on the copper surface; the nitro groups additionally strengthen intermolecular interactions between NBT and PEG. MD simulations further confirm that NBT anchors onto the Cu(111) surface predominantly through these $\Nu { \cal O } _ { 2 }$ groups and the tetrazolium ring, while co-adsorbed PEG enhances the overall adsorption strength of NBT. The electroplating experiment demonstrates that NBT can act as an effective leveler for microvia superfilling. Moreover, XPS analyses further confirm the synergistic co-adsorption of NBT and PEG and verify that the $\Nu { \cal O } _ { 2 }$ groups and tetrazolium rings are the dominant adsorption sites of NBT. Collectively, the electroplating, XPS, electrochemical, DFT, and MD findings clarify the structure–activity relationship of NBT and provide rational guidelines for designing next-generation copper-plating levelers.

surface_text: Industrial practice predominantly relies on organic additive systems to locally regulate the deposition rate for achieving superfilling of microvias. In two-component systems the competitive adsorption of a suppressor and an accelerator is often sufficient for sub-100 nm Damascene features [7–9]; larger microvias, however, require a third component—a leveler— to suppress copper deposition at high-current-density sites (feature mouths and protrusions), thereby ensuring void-free bottom-up growth and surface planarization [10–12]. Among the numerous levelers reported, Janus Green B (JGB) is the most classic, as it can achieve not only superfilling in microvias [13] but also high throwing power (TP) electroplated in through-holes [14]. surface_text: As is well known, nitro blue tetrazolium chloride (NBT), a commercially available tetrazolium dye, has demonstrated excellent performance as a leveler in through-hole copper filling [28–30]. In contrast, blind microvias present a far more challenging environment: with only one opening, electrolyte circulation is severely restricted, the diffusion layer thickens, and a pronounced ohmic and activation overpotential gradient develops. These factors make void-free filling in blind microvias significantly more difficult than in through-holes. To date, however, the suitability of NBT for blind-microvia superfilling has not been reported, nor has its structure–performance relationship been elucidated—an omission that limits the molecular-level insight into tetrazolium-based levelers and the rational design of cost-effective additives. Accordingly, NBT was chosen as the leveler in this study to assess its effectiveness in copper superfilling of microvias, of which the molecular structure is shown in Figure 1. By combining electrochemical analyses, electroplating experiments, X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS), MD simulations, and DFT calculations, we elucidate how NBT’s NO<sub>2</sub> groups and tetrazolium ring govern the adsorption on Cu(111) and synergism with PEG and other species. The insights provide rational guidelines for engineering the next-generation, robust, and economical levelers.

surface_text: The additives utilized in the acidic sulfate copper plating process primarily consist of chloride ions (Cl-) [12], accelerators, suppressors and levelers. These additives interact with one another to enhance the performance of resulting formed copper plating layer [13, 14, 5, 15–17]. Previous research on suppressors for acid copper electroplating has predominantly focused on polymers and surfactants with diverse molecular structures. For instance, polyethylene glycol (PEG)-based polymers have been widely studied and utilized as suppressors due to their ability to adsorb on the copper surface and inhibit the deposition reaction [18, 19]. However, their high molecular weight and complex synthesis processes often lead to issues such as poor bath stability and dificulty in waste treatment, raising environmental concerns. Polyetheramine (PEP) has also been investigated as a potential suppressor, leveraging its unique amine-containing structure that allows for specific interactions with the copper surface [17, 20]. While PEP shows promise in adjusting the deposition rate, its relatively high cost and limited biodegradability pose challenges for large—scale industrial application. Additionally, ethylene—propylene copolymer (EPE) has been explored, as its alternating structure can provide a balance between hydrophobic and hydrophilic properties, influencing the deposition behavior [21, 22]. Nevertheless, EPE may sufer from inconsistent performance under varying electroplating conditions, and its efect on the quality of microvia filling in high—aspect—ratio scenarios remains suboptimal. Moreover, some non—ionic surfactants like Triton X—series have been investigated, but they may exhibit limited eficiency in microvia filling under high— aspect—ratio conditions and can also pose potential toxicity risks.

surface_text: Based on the research on Tween compounds as eco— friendly suppressors for acid copper electroplating in microvia applications, several key guidelines are proposed. Firstly, when selecting Tween compounds, factors like their hydrophilic—lipophilic balance, molecular weight, and branching structure should be carefully considered to ensure proper adsorption and inhibitory efects. Secondly, concentration optimization is crucial, as both too low and too high concentrations can negatively impact microvia filling quality, thus requiring systematic studies to find the optimal balance. surface_text: For through-hole plating, the relatively complex pulse electroplating technique has been commonly employed<sup>12–14</sup>. Ning et al.<sup>16</sup> utilised horizontal pulse copper electroplating technology to successfully achieve conformal thickening of high-aspect-ratio through-holes and super-filling of blind holes, ultimately obtaining a smooth copper layer. Compared to the complex pulse electroplating process, direct current (DC) copper electroplating ofers advantages such as lower equipment costs, simpler operational parameters and higher process stability. Liu et al.<sup>9</sup> developed an electroplating solution formulation suitable for the simultaneous filling of through-holes and blind holes, which can be implemented using only a direct current (DC) power supply. Additionally, they optimised the process by improving the pattern plating method, thereby minimising the thickness of the surface copper. Zhao et al.<sup>17</sup> employed 1-dodecyl-2-methyl-3-benzylimidazolium chloride (DMBI) as a leveller, successfully achieving conformal thickening in through-holes and void-free filling in blind holes. In situ ATR-SEIRAS spectroscopy and electrochemical experiments revealed that DMBI inhibits the electroreduction of copper ions by competing with SPS. Currently, the simultaneous electroplating process for through-holes and blind holes primarily focuses on achieving conformal thickening of through-holes. However, this conformal thickening approach may lead to reduced signal transmission reliability and insuficient thermal performance during the long-term use of HDI<sup>18–20</sup>. To address these issues, it is necessary to achieve complete filling of through-holes. Therefore, this study aims to develop an acidic sulphate copper plating process based on a low-voltage DC power supply to achieve simultaneous and complete filling of through-holes and blind holes.

With the addition of SPS or SPS + Cl<sup>−</sup>, the resulting grains noticeably increase in size, with the deposition mode lying between preferred orientation and a layered structure.<sup>22</sup> The accelerator is primarily a small molecule compound containing sulfur, usually consisting of two parts. One part comprises thiol or disulfide bonds, and the other part is a sulfonic acid salt group. surface_text: 4.1. Halide Ions. Halide ions are an essential component in the plating solution of the acidic copper plating system, commonly dominated by chloride ions. It mainly exists in the form of sodium chloride or hydrochloric acid in the copper plating solution. Although its required content in the plating solution is relatively low, it plays a significant role. Chloride ions enhance the conductivity of the system, facilitate the dissolution of phosphor copper anodes, reduce the formation of “copper powder” due to incomplete anode dissolution, improve the brightness and leveling ability of the coating, and enhance coating quality. Chloride ions play a dual role: inducing the capture of copper ions by the inner layer electron transfer of the accelerator MPS sulfonate ${ \mathrm { R } } { - } S { \mathrm { O } } _ { 3 } ^ { - }$ , synergizing with the accelerator MPS to accelerate the deposition of copper ions on the cathode surface; also acting as an inhibitor, adsorbing on the cathode surface $\begin{array} { r l } { \mathsf { a s } \textbf { a } ^ { \infty } \mathbf { h o o l } \breve { \mathbf { k } ^ { \prime \prime } } } \end{array}$ to enable the inhibitor to function properly $( { \mathrm { F i g u r e } } \ 5 )$ . Chloride ions can also serve as a “chlorine bridge” between the electrode surface and $\boldsymbol { \mathrm { C u } } ^ { + }$ . This increases the concentration of subcopper ions on the electrode surface, reduces the double-layer capacitance, weakens polar ization, lowers nucleation rates, ultimately achieving favorable conditions for crystal nucleus growth. Research also suggests that certain leveling agents using I<sup>−</sup> as the counteranion exhibit significantly enhanced inhibitory capabilities compared to $\mathrm { C l ^ { - } }$ as the anion. surface_text: 4.3. Inhibitors. In electroplating additives, inhibitors achieve the suppression of surface copper deposition by adsorbing onto the copper surface, enhancing cathodic polarization, and inhibiting the deposition of copper on the surface. Inhibitors are generally polyether substances with a certain molecular weight. Common inhibitors include polyethylene glycol (PEG), polypropylene glycol (PPG), and a copolymer of ethylene glycol and 1, 2-Propanediol (EPE). The molecular weight of PEG is around 6000 to 10000. Inhibitors have a larger molecular weight and are easily consumed during the electrodeposition process. Therefore, during electroplating, inhibitors primarily exhibit a gradient distribution on the surface ofthe plated piece. For PCB electroplated copper pillars, the bottom of microblind holes is relatively distant from the bulk solution, leading to a reduced distribution of inhibitors in this area. The concentration of inhibitors at the opening of the hole is closer to the concentration of inhibitors in the bulk solution. Additionally, as these polyol substances are excellent surfactants, they also function as wetting agents in copper electroplating. When the amount of inhibitor added is too small, resulting in insuficient wetting of the board surface, it causes the surface to appear red and dull.

This work systematically studied the influence of the Acid Blue 1 (AB1) leveler on blind microvia filling. This study systematically investigates the application of a novel leveler, thiazolyl blue (MTT), for PCB THs’ electroplating, successfully realizing high-quality conformal deposition in high-aspect-ratio (10:1) THs. Electrochemical analyses demonstrate that MTT significantly enhances the cathodic polarization and efectively inhibits the reduction of Cu<sup>2+</sup>. Meanwhile, microscopic morphological characterizations confirm

surface_text: that MTT exhibits excellent leveling capability, reducing the surface roughness of the copper deposit to as low as 0.147 μm. Furthermore, density functional theory (DFT) calculations reveal that the high inhibitory eficiency of MTT originates from the dominant interfacial adsorption of MTT at the cathode. with the bulk cation-π interaction with $\mathrm { C u } ^ { 2 + }$ contributing as a minor secondary effect at the microscopic level. Crystallographic and interfacial wettability analyses further indicate that MTT effectively refines the grain size and promotes the preferential growth of the Cu(200) plane while improving the wettability of the plating bath. Based on these results, a competitive interfacial polarization remodeling mechanism governed by multiphysics coupling is proposed to elucidate the intrinsic role of MTT in promoting conformal through-hole deposition. The local current density at the via opening is significantly higher than that at the center, accompanied by severe mass transfer limitations of Cu<sup>2+</sup> within the hole. This multiphysics imbalance frequently triggers the “dog-bone” defect, characterized by excessive copper accumulation at the via opening and excessively thin deposits on the inner walls.<sup>11</sup> Such nonuniform deposition severely compromises the electrical and mechanical performance of the interconnected structures, constituting a universal bottleneck in the high-density interconnect (HDI) industry.<sup>12</sup> To overcome this challenge, it is imperative to introduce suppressors, accelerators, and levelers into the acidic copper sulfate bath.<sup>13</sup> The precise synergistic and competitive adsorption among these three additives dynamically modulates the deposition kinetics at diferent spatial locations within the TH, ultimately achieving high-quality conformal interconnection.

surface_text: Typically, polyether macromolecules (e.g., polyethylene glycol, PEG) serve as suppressors; bridged by chloride ions, they profoundly enhance cathodic polarization and retard copper growth.<sup>14</sup> Sulfonate compounds bearing thiol or disulfide groups (e.g., bis(3-sulfopropyl) disulfide, SPS) act as accelerators: they capture Cu<sup>2+</sup> at the cathode interface and lower the activation barrier for its reduction.<sup>15</sup> Among the plating formulations, the leveler plays the most critica interfacial regulatory role. By preferentially adsorbing at strongly convected regions (e.g., the opening), the leveler establishes a localized high-impedance barrier that inhibits overplating,<sup>16−18</sup> thereby compelling the spatial electric field lines to redistribute deeper into TH.<sup>19−21</sup> To date, various commercial dyes have been reported as levelers (e.g., Janus Green B, tetrazolium blue chloride, PAN).<sup>22−24</sup> Meanwhile, some researchers have devoted eforts to the synthesis of nove polymeric levelers (e.g., VIBDGE, PBDGE, Sudan-QNL). 25−27 Nevertheless, each of the aforementioned levelers exhibits specific limitations. Polymeric levelers such as VIBDGE and PBDGE, despite their promising performance, typically require multistep synthesis and tedious purification procedures, which considerably increase the production cost and hinder their practical scalability. Commercial dye-based levelers (e.g., Janus Green B) are readily accessible and have been widely adopted in industry with proven efectiveness; however, as the aspec ratio of through-holes continues to increase, further enhance ment of throwing power remains highly desirable to ensure the thickness uniformity and long-term reliability of the copper interconnects. In this regard, MTT ofers a compelling combination of advantages: it is a commercially available, of the-shelf reagent that can be directly procured at low cost entirely eliminating the need for custom synthesis or purification, and as will be demonstrated in Section 3.5, it delivers a throwing power (TP = 96.8%) that markedly outperforms the conventional leveler JGB (TP = 84.5%) under identical bath composition and process conditions. surface_text: To comprehensively evaluate the through-hole filling capability of MTT, the thickness uniformity of its electrodeposited copper layers within printed circuit board (PCB) throughholes was systematically characterized. In the PCB through hole electroplating process, Throwing Power (TP) serves as the pivotal quantitative index for evaluating the internal deposit thickness uniformity and evaluating the quality of the copper interconnects. The magnitude of the TP directly dictates the electrical reliability and long-term service lifespan of the 3D interconnected structures. Figures 5a,b, and S6 display high-resolution metallographic cross-sectional optical micrographs of the through-holes after electrodeposition under various MTT concentrations. At a constant current density of $2 \mathrm { A } / \mathrm { d } \mathrm { m } ^ { 2 } ,$ when VMS exclusively contains the accelerator SPS and the suppressor PEG (Figure 5a), the TP value of the through-hole is only 25.2%. At this juncture, a distinct geometric disparity exists between the deposit thickness at the opening and that in the central region, resulting in a severe “dog-bone” morphological defect that fundamentally fails to meet the electrical reliability requirements for high-density interconnects. Remarkably, with the introduction of MTT into the plating system, this geometric efect of uneven deposit distribution is efectively suppressed, and the overall coating morphology transits almost into a conformal deposition. As illustrated in Figure 5b, upon adding an optimal MTT concentration of 50 mg/L, the TP value increases to 96.8%. This visually dictates that MTT bridges the thickness gap between the surface opening and the deep interior, achieving high-quality conformal thickening of the copper layer within the through-hole.

surface_text: To further benchmark the leveling performance of MTT against a well-established commercial leveler, a comparative through-hole electroplating experiment was conducted using 50 mg/L Janus Green B (JGB) under identical bath composition and process conditions. Nevertheless, the overall copper deposit thickness within the through-hole remains noticeably thin compared to that achieved with MTT, yielding a TP value of approximately 84.5%. surface_text: Coupling the theoretical elucidation of the MTT inhibition mechanism in Section 3.3 with previous studies, competitive interfacial polarization remodeling driven by a multiphysics coupling mechanism was proposed to unveil the intrinsic influence of MTT. As portrayed in the schematic mechanism (Figure 5c), governed by the coupling of fluid dynamics (convective mass transfer) and electrochemical kinetics, MTT, PEG, and SPS undergo competitive adsorption at the solid− liquid interface within the through-hole. This induces a spatially diferentiated distribution of polarization resistance, reshaping the potential field across the inner surface of the through-hole. Specifically, propelled by the forced convection at the hole opening, MTT rapidly accumulates and adsorbs in this region via convection-dependent adsorption (CDA).<sup>54,55</sup> Concurrently, MTT interacts synergistically with the PEG polymer chains and the bridging chloride ions to form a dense ternary synergistic suppression film on the copper substrate. This compact adsorption layer triggers a notable increase in the local polarization resistance at the opening. The resulting elevated electrochemical reaction barrier efectively suppresses the electroreduction kinetics of ${ \mathrm { C u } } ^ { 2 + }$ in this vicinity. Consequently, the increased polarization resistance at the orifice compels the spatial electric field lines $( \mathrm { i . e . , }$ the primary current distribution) to redistribute toward the deep interior of the through-hole, which is situated in a weak convection zone.<sup>56,57</sup> Through this polarization remodeling efect, the inherent Ohmic potential drop caused by the geometric aspect ratio of the through-hole is compensated. Simultaneously, a steady-state difusion flux of $\mathrm { C u } ^ { 2 + }$ directed into the hole is sustained, ultimately driving the realization of a conformal through-hole deposition.

surface_text: In summary, this study systematically investigated the application performance and multiphysics coupling mechanisms of MTT, acting as a leveler for copper electrodeposition in PCB through-holes. Electrochemical evaluations demon strate that MTT significantly enhances cathodic polarization via a convection-dependent interfacial adsorption. Meanwhile, microscopic morphological characterization confirms that MTT exhibits excellent leveling capability, significantly reducing the surface roughness of the copper deposit to 0.147 μm. Such a smooth surface topography is highly beneficial for mitigating the skin efect and lowering insertion loss during high-frequency signal transmission. Density functional theory analysis further elucidates that the microscopic origin of this robust inhibitory behavior lies primarily in the strong interfacial adsorption of MTT at the cathode, with the bulk cation−π interaction with ${ \mathrm { C u } } ^ { 2 + }$ contributing as a minor secondary efect. Phase structure and interface analysis illustrate that an optimal MTT concentration (50 mg/L) not only efectively refines the crystalline grain size and promotes the preferential growth of the Cu(200) plane but also decreases the solid−liquid interfacial contact angle to ${ 5 4 . 6 } ^ { \circ } ,$ thereby fundamentally suppressing the generation of macroscopic morphological defects. Ultimately, in practical throughhole electroplating applications, the competitive adsorption among MTT, PEG, and SPS induces a spatially diferentiated remodeling of polarization resistance. By establishing a high impedance barrier at the forced-convection orifice region, the inherent Ohmic potential drop within the through-holes is efectively compensated. Driven by this multiphysical coupling mechanism, the TP value of through-holes is substantially elevated from 25.2% to 96.8%, markedly outperforming the conventional leveler JGB (TP = 84.5%) under identical conditions, successfully achieving high-quality conformal deposition and providing a theoretical and practical basis for the fabrication of highly reliable, high-frequency 3D interconnected PCB structures.

surface_text: Additives are widely used to modulate the conditions of plating in electrodeposition. In particular, when performing feature filling, additives are essential components that cause a variation in the deposition speed depending on the deposition spots, thereby enabling the performance of superconformal filling. Copper bottom-up filling electrodeposition is performed using a threeadditive system consisting of a suppressor, an accelerator, and a leveler. Many studies have been conducted on the behavior of additives and their growth mechanisms; however, various additives are still being developed for copper electrodeposition.<sup>19–24</sup> I n the case of nickel, one of the iron group metals, there have also been many studies on additives for superconformal filling. Polyethyleneimine (PEI) and benzimidazole derivatives, such as 2-mercaptobenzimidazole (MBI) and 2-mercapto-5-benzimidazolesulfonic acid (MBIS), were shown to yield void-free feature filling.<sup>25–27</sup> Conversely, for cobalt, there are studies on the additives and mechanisms for cobalt bottom-up filling, although these are still insufficient. In cobalt bottom-up electrodeposition, some studies explain the mechanism based on the S-shaped negative differential resistance theory<sup>28,29</sup> and the deposition speed difference due to complex formation,<sup>30</sup> which has been suggested in copper bottom-up filling studies. Studies explaining the mechanism based on the interaction with the hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) involved in cobalt reduction have also been reported.<sup>31,32</sup>

surface_text: With the increasing integration of integrated circuits, the size of transistors has reached the nm level. Due to the influence of size effect, the resistivity of Cu interconnectors increases exponentially when the line width below 14 nm. So new materials are needed to replace metal Cu as interconnects. Metal Co has attracted widespread attention because of its short mean free path of electrons, low resistivity, stable performance and low electromigration. However, due to the short development time of the new chip technology and the immature process of new alternative materials, further analysis and study of the inhibitor and the molecular structure of the inhibitor suitable for the metal Co filling process are still needed. Therefore, studying the seamless filling Co technology has very important theoretical and practical value. According to theoretical calculation and Hull cell experiment, this paper compared the dispersion ability of plating bath after adding additives with different structures and their inhibition ability on Co plating bath, determined the molecular structure suitable for use as a Co plating inhibitor, and discussed the electrochemical behavior and filling effect of the inhibitor in the plating solution. Finally, a metal Co plating process suitable for micron level blind hole filling was verified.

surface_text: 金属 Co 具有较低的平均电子自由程，因此作为纳米级别的互连线时，相较于体电阻率，其变化较小。作为互连材料，Co 仅需要一层阻抗层，而 Cu 则需要更厚的阻抗层和粘附层。此外，Co 的抗电迁移性能也比 Cu 更优异，因此作为替代材料，Co 在纳米级别互连中更具有优势，可以作为互连材料代替 Cu。对于 Co 的制备过程，仍以电沉积为主，这是因为只需要添加少量的抑制剂就可以实现 Co的无缝填充，因此对于添加剂的研究和选择也是目前的研究重点。

surface_text: 尽管目前有一些关于金属 Co 填充过程中的添加剂的研究，但是对于如何选择以及选择何种结构的添加剂，仍没有定论。而且文献中报道的抑制剂多为聚合物，这是基于长链结构容易在电极表面吸附，阻碍 Co 沉积，但同时又面临一个问题，Co 作为替代金属，主要用于纳米级别的互连的，而长链结构的大分子容易在孔口处堆叠致使沉积过程离子传输受阻，容易导致盲孔内出现缝隙。而小分子作为添加剂时，则需要较高的浓度以达到无缝填充的抑制效果，这种情况下容易导致 Co 镀层中出现 C，N 和 O 等原子掺杂，进而使 Co 镀层电阻率进一步升高，因此选择一种合适分子量的抑制剂也是提高 Co 镀层性能的关键。本文首先根据文献调研筛选了多种不同结构的添加剂作为抑制剂，研究其对 Co 填充过程影响，然后利用 MD 模拟和 QC 计算分析不同结构的添加剂，通过与实验测试对比分析适合 Co 填充的分子结构，从而确定合适的添加剂分子结构与模拟计算之间的关系，为以后在不同尺寸的盲孔或通孔进行填充时提供一种可用的添加剂筛选方案。此外，由于 $\mathrm { C o } ^ { 2 + }$ 还原过程中同时发生 HER，本文还研究了抑制剂对氢还原过程的影响，并通过电化学测试和填充实验分析了 HER 过程在填充过程中的作用，为以后 Co 在纳米级别盲孔中的填充过程提供了一种可用的机理模型。
review_notes: explicit domain, action and additive/chemical cue; expert adjudication required

surface_text: 大马士革电镀铜工艺主要是利用不同添加剂的相互作用，使铜离子在盲孔内外沉积时出现镀速差，其经典的组成配方为：加速剂为双（硫丙基）二硫化物（SPS），整平剂为健那绿（JGB）以及抑制剂聚乙二醇（PEG）。基础镀液组成为 $\mathrm { C u S O _ { 4 } }$ 和 $\mathrm { H } _ { 2 } \mathrm { S O } _ { 4 }$ 。在大规模集成电路中，镀液的配方往往采用低铜高酸的基础镀液和不同浓度的添加剂以达到无缝填充的效果<sup>[28]</sup>，作用机理如图 1-4。
review_notes: explicit domain, action and additive/chemical cue; expert adjudication required

surface_text: 如图 1-4 所示，抑制剂 PEG 与溶液中还原的 $\mathrm { C u } ^ { 2 \cdot }$ 形成稳定 PEG-Cu(I)-Cl<sup>-</sup>配合物，从而抑制 Cu 成核沉积，但是随着沉积的进行，盲孔或沟槽外表面 PEG浓度变化不大，而底部 PEG 由于掺杂进镀层或被击穿导致浓度降低，此时 SPS吸附在底部阴极表面，逐渐分解为 MPS，然后与还原的一价 Cu 和 Cl<sup>-</sup>形成的MPS-Cu(I)-Cl<sup>-</sup>配合物吸附在阴极表面，其中 S 原子作为活性位点促进 Cu 成核沉积。而 JGB 整平剂被认为是吸附在开口处，从而使开口处的沉积过程延迟到最后的封孔<sup>[29]</sup>。在后续的发展中，大马士革镀铜工艺几乎一直按照这一机理进行，只是在研究过程中选择不同的可替换的添加剂来适应不同尺寸的盲孔或沟槽。
review_notes: explicit domain, action and additive/chemical cue; expert adjudication required

surface_text: 其次，自从化学镀 Co 被报道出来<sup>[65]</sup>，利用化学镀的方式同样可以实现 Co的填充过程。但是目前所报道的化学镀 Co 主要集中在将 Co 作为粘附层沉积在阻挡层 TaN 上，以提高 Cu 互连线的附着力<sup>[66-69]</sup>。相对于电镀的方式，化学镀可以在非导体的基底上沉积，因为在沉积过程中会在基底上首先吸附还原性的离子/原子，然后促使 Co 离子还原沉积<sup>[70-72]</sup>。但是，化学镀制备的 Cu 填充线，其在沟槽或通孔内的镀层厚度往往低于外表面的厚度，这种方式更适合制备粘附层或阻抗层。因此，如果通过化学镀的方法进行 Co 无缝填充时，还需要考虑添加剂与化学镀的还原剂之间的相互作用，添加剂的作用机理也更加复杂。此外，研究表明采用 ALD 的方法制备的单层 Ru 原子，可以作为互连材料的阻挡层<sup>[73,</sup> <sup>74]</sup>。因此，相较于化学镀的方式，利用电沉积的方法制备 Co 互连线更便捷（省去了还原/活化过程），操作流程更简单，更经济实用。所以本文通过在镀液中加入合适的抑制剂，利用电沉积的方式制备 Co 填充层。
review_notes: explicit domain, action and additive/chemical cue; expert adjudication required

surface_text: Huang等人<sup>[107-109]</sup>利用二肟类化合物作为抑制剂研究金属Co的沉积过程，通过 CV 曲线发现，还原电位达到沉积电势时，电流密度出现急剧增加，出现S 负微分电阻现象，如图 1-14 所示。二肟类化合物可以与 $\mathrm { C o } ^ { 2 + }$ 形成稳定的配合物，抑制了 Co 还原沉积，同时对氢析出过程有加速作用。通过电势瞬态曲线发现，抑制剂浓度的增加，瞬态电势逐渐降低。这种抑制方式能够在 Co 填充时，在盲孔内形成浓度梯度，从而可以实现金属 Co 的无缝填充。通过电流瞬态曲线发现，添加二肟类抑制剂使 Co 呈现出三维渐进成核过程。
review_notes: explicit domain, action and additive/chemical cue; expert adjudication required
